stops.name: Damascus, illness and the sultan's death
stops.campa: Nine weeks after the gates opened to him the illnesses close in together — a cough, a flux of the bowels, the old gout in his legs — and the sultan is carried to a small room of the Dar al-Qasaba inside the citadel. It is the room where his uncle Salah al-Din died forty-five years before. He has outlived Saladin's whole generation, outlived al-Mu'azzam and al-Ashraf both, turned back both crusades that came at Egypt on terms mostly his own. No enemy stands over the bed; it is the exhaustion of long rule that takes him, on a Thursday night, in his sixtieth year.

stops.name: Damascus, burial, and the house of Ayyub unravels
stops.campa: He is buried the next day inside the citadel where he died, amid the mourning of a dynasty that, within days, resumes the quarrel he spent his reign suppressing: his sons as-Salih Ayyub in the east and al-Adil II in Cairo divide the inheritance he tried to keep whole, and the Ayyubid house slides back into the fratricidal politics of Saladin's own sons two generations before. The peace with the Franks he built stone by traded stone will outlive him barely a decade before the Mamluks he first brought to Egypt as slave-soldiers take the sultanate from his line — but for twenty years, a war-torn coast knew, because of him, more truce than battle.
